d: Adaptive timestepping automatically assigns physical parts to varying simulation timesteps.
h:
The Roblox physics engine simulates all parts inside the 3D workspace through Newton's second law of motion. This law of motion is solved over time via timesteps and a single timestep is done within a worldstep in Roblox.

By default, Roblox simulates physics at 240 Hz. Given cycles of approximately 60 frames per second, around 4 worldsteps are advanced per frame. With adaptive timestepping, the physics engine automatically assigns parts to three "solver islands" by varying their simulation timestep, with an emphasis on 60 Hz for best performance. However, parts that are "harder" to solve will use a faster timestep like 240 Hz to ensure physical stability.

Assignment criterions are subject to change, but parts assigned to the 240 Hz island include assemblies with high velocity values, high acceleration values, and complex mechanisms that are hard to solve.

Enable adaptive mode

To enable adaptive timestepping in Studio:

  1. In the Explorer window, select the Workspace object.

  1. In the Properties window, locate PhysicsSteppingMethod and select Adaptive.

To observe the timestepping process in action, you can open the Studio Microprofiler (CtrlF6; ⌘F6). Once the game is running, press CtrlP (⌘P) to pause at the current frame.

Under the scope named physicsStepped, observe that the scope name of worldStep now reads worldStep - Adaptive.

Hovering your cursor above LDLPGSSolver::solve will reveal the status of how many islands belong in each frequency bucket; 1dt Islands (240 Hz), 2dt Islands (120 Hz) and 4dt Islands (60 Hz).

Debug visualization

During testing, it may be useful to visualize frequencies for simulated parts. To enable this option:

  1. Open Studio Settings.
  2. From the Physics tab, enable Are Timesteps Shown.

Once enabled, simulated parts will be outlined by their current simulation rate. If a part stops being simulated, either via the sleep system or a network ownership change, the part will no longer be outlined.

Fixed-rate scenarios

Adaptive timestepping can improve physics performance by up to 2.5 times and it is recommended in most cases. However, some games should use Fixed mode (240 Hz), including:

Games that require highly accurate simulations and stability, such as racing games, "destruction" simulations, or games featuring complex mechanisms like tanks.

Simulations where most parts default to the 240 Hz solver island (red outlines during debugging). When 240 Hz islands interact with islands of different frequencies (60–120 Hz), those islands are converted to 240 Hz with an overhead that may negate any performance gains resulting from adaptive timestepping.

kid.simple: Physics in Roblox is calculated in lots of tiny steps every second. Adaptive timestepping lets the engine use fewer steps for easy objects and more steps for tricky ones. This can make physics run up to 2.5 times faster. You turn it on with one setting on Workspace, but some games, like racing games, should keep the fixed mode.
kid.analogy: It is like a flip-book animation: a calm scene only needs a few pages per second, but a fast car crash needs many more pages so it looks right. Adaptive timestepping gives each object just as many pages as it needs.
keyPoints: By default Roblox calculates physics 240 times per second, which is about 4 physics steps for each 60-frames-per-second frame.
Adaptive timestepping sorts parts into three groups ('solver islands'): 60, 120, or 240 steps per second.
Most parts go to 60 Hz for speed. Fast-moving, quickly speeding up, or complicated mechanisms go to 240 Hz to stay stable.
To turn it on: select Workspace in the Explorer, then in Properties set `PhysicsSteppingMethod` to Adaptive.
To see which rate each part uses: open Studio Settings, go to the Physics tab, and turn on Are Timesteps Shown. Parts get colored outlines.
You can also check it in the Microprofiler (Ctrl+F6 or Cmd+F6), where worldStep will read worldStep - Adaptive.
Use Fixed mode (always 240 Hz) for games needing very accurate physics, like racing, destruction, or tanks, or when most parts end up in the 240 Hz group anyway.

terms.timestep: The small slice of time between two physics calculations. At 240 Hz each step is 1/240 of a second.
terms.worldstep: One full physics update of the world, done once per timestep.
terms.Hz (hertz): Times per second. 240 Hz means 240 times every second; 60 Hz means 60 times.
terms.frame: One picture drawn on your screen. Games usually draw about 60 frames each second.
terms.solver island: A group of parts that the physics engine solves together at the same step rate.
terms.Newton's second law: The rule that force equals mass times acceleration. Roblox uses it to figure out how hard pushes change how things move.
terms.Microprofiler: A Studio tool that shows how long each part of the game's work takes, frame by frame.
terms.overhead: Extra work the computer has to do. Mixing 240 Hz parts with slower ones adds overhead that can cancel out the speed boost.

watchOut: Do not turn on Adaptive for a game that needs super precise physics, like a racing game. Things may feel less stable.
If almost every part shows red (240 Hz) outlines, adaptive mode is not helping. Switch back to Fixed.
Parts that stop being outlined are not broken; they may just be asleep or owned by another player's computer.
